name: Munji

catalog_citation: Williamson, Paul. 2017. Munji (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 47(2): 213-218. doi:10.1017/S0025100316000256
catalog_locator: section 'Stress', pp. 216-217 (pp. 4-5 of the saved Cambridge PDF rendered and)
catalog_quote: Both long and short vowels may be stressed. In unstressed syllables, there is a tendency toward neutralization of short vowels. [heading: Stress] Stress is usually on the first syllable of nouns, but there are a number of exceptions where the stress placement is part of the underlying form of word and is not predictable. Words are stressed on their stems and not on their suffixes. However, the negative verbal prefix, [t͡ʃʊ-], is always stressed. Otherwise, two-syllable verb stems are stressed on the second syllable. For a number of verbs, the present tense stem contains one syllable and the past tense stem contains two syllables, so the stress placement corresponds to a difference in the past and non-past stems (/ˈwɪʃc-əm/ ‘stand up.prs.1sg’ /wɪʃˈcɔj-əm/ ‘stand up.pst.1sg’).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is anchored to the stem, never to suffixes: nouns are by default stressed on the first syllable (with a residue of lexically fixed exceptions, e.g. /pɪˈɡa/ 'morning' vs /ˈpɪɡə/ 'hair'), and disyllabic verb stems are stressed on their second syllable; the negative prefix t͡ʃʊ-/t͡ʃɪ- always takes primary stress. Stress is therefore morphologically governed rather than fixed to a syllable position across the whole vocabulary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in Williamson 2017 or Williamson & Williamson. Morgenstierne 1938 §165 (p. 105) speculates only historically about 'presence or absence of a secondary accent' as a cause of prefix vowel outcomes.
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns: 'a number of exceptions where the stress placement is part of the underlying form of word and is not predictable'. Verbs: negative prefix always stressed; stress differs between present and past stems; Williamson & Williamson (pp. 30-31) add a class of verbs where stress alone distinguishes present (ˈavəɾ-əm 'I bring') from past (aˈvəɾ-əm 'I brought'), and stress distinguishes the perfect feminine (root stress) from the masculine participle (suffix stress -əˈɣə). Morgenstierne 1938 p. 34: 'Word stress is weak, and to some extent dominated by sentence stress', with earlier recorders (Gauthiot, Zarubin) disagreeing about placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; based on a 3,000-item lexical database and recordings from northern (Shahran) and southern (Tili) dialect speakers; JIPA illustration recordings from a northern-dialect speaker. Morgenstierne's 1938 remark that word stress is weak and partly dominated by sentence stress is the only phrase-level comment.
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 2017 and Williamson & Williamson describe Munji of the Kuran wa Munjan valley, Badakhshan (both northern and southern dialects; the JIPA recordings are from a northern-dialect speaker from Shahran) = munj1244. Morgenstierne 1938 treats Yidgha-Munji jointly; his §39 stress remark applies to both Yidgha (yidg1239) and Munji, with examples marked Y (Yidgha) and M/Mm (Munji, Mamalgha).

sources.note: Section 'Stress' pp. 216-217: stress usually on the first syllable of nouns with unpredictable lexical exceptions; words stressed on stems not suffixes; negative verbal prefix always stressed; two-syllable verb stems stressed on the second syllable; present/past stems differ in stress placement (/ˈwɪʃc-əm/ vs /wɪʃˈcɔj-əm/). Both long and short vowels may be stressed; short vowels tend to neutralize when unstressed.

sources.note: Section 'Stress' pp. 29-31: 'For nouns, stress is usually on the first syllable. But there are a few examples of stress playing a part in distinguishing lexical items: /pɪˈɡa/ morning, /ˈpɪɡə/ hair. For verbs, stress is on the stem. If the stem is two syllables, then the stress is on the second syllable of the stem.' Stress is grammatically contrastive for a group of verbs (present ˈavəɾ-əm vs past aˈvəɾ-əm) and between perfect-tense feminine and masculine participle forms; 'Other than participles, stress occurs on the roots of words and not on their suffixes. sources.citation: Morgenstierne, Georg. 1938. Indo-Iranian Frontier Languages, Vol. II: Iranian Pamir Languages (Yidgha-Munji, Sanglechi-Ishkashmi and Wakhi). Oslo: Instituttet for Sammenlignende Kulturforskning, Serie B XXXV
sources.note: Yidgha-Munji, Phonetic System §39 'Stress', pp. 34-35 (p. 57): 'Word stress is weak, and to some extent dominated by sentence stress.' Notes that Gauthiot and Zarubin differ on accent placement in Munji (Gauthiot inclining to final stress), his own notations often disagree with both and are not always consistent; Yidgha often stresses a later syllable than Munji. Historical 'Accent and Contraction' §§162 sqq. pp. 103-105: present accentuation cannot be derived from any ancient system; most words are of two accent types.
No stress information; its phonology section cites Williamson & Williamson (zabanha.af) and Williamson 2017 JIPA, which led to the primary sources above.
